title: Foundations: polynomials, fields, and Galois groups
subject: foundations
summary: An introduction to irreducibility, algebraic extensions, and the action of the Galois group on roots, with examples and connections to arithmetic and geometry.
questionsAnswered: How does an irreducible polynomial define a field extension?
How do irreducible factors correspond to Galois orbits?
What does the Galois group tell us about an equation?
How are these questions related to finite fields, local fields, and polynomial families?

sections.title: From equations to fields
sections.body:
To study a polynomial, one first chooses its coefficient field. One then asks whether it factors, which field contains its roots, and which permutations of the roots preserve their algebraic relations. These questions lead from polynomial arithmetic to field extensions and Galois groups.

Consider \(x^3-2\). It has no rational root, so it is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\). Adjoining its real root gives a field of degree three. To obtain all three roots, one must also adjoin a primitive cube root of unity. The resulting field has degree six, and its automorphisms realize all six permutations of the roots. Irreducibility, the degree of a field generated by one root, and the Galois group describe different parts of this example.

This article gives an overview. Field extensions develops the construction and arithmetic of fields generated by roots. The Galois correspondence explains how subgroups describe intermediate fields and changes of the coefficient field.

citations.note: Field extensions and explicit Galois-group calculations.

sections.title: Irreducibility and the ground field
sections.body:
A nonconstant polynomial \(f\in K[x]\) is irreducible over \(K\) if it cannot be written as a product of two polynomials of positive degree in \(K[x]\). Every nonconstant polynomial over a field factors uniquely into monic irreducible polynomials, apart from its leading coefficient and the order of the factors.

Irreducibility depends on \(K\). For example, \(x^2-2\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\), but

\[x^2-2=(x-\sqrt2)(x+\sqrt2)\]

over \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)\). Over \(\mathbb C\), every nonconstant polynomial is a product of linear factors. Over \(\mathbb R\), irreducible polynomials have degree one or two. Over a finite field, irreducible polynomials occur in every positive degree.

For a polynomial in several variables, absolute irreducibility means irreducibility after extending the coefficient field to an algebraic closure. This is a substantial condition in several variables. In one variable, only degree-one polynomials are absolutely irreducible.

citations.note: Polynomial factorization and algebraic extensions.
Finite extensions of finite fields; irreducible polynomials are obtained from generators.

sections.title: Gauss’s lemma
sections.body:
The content of a nonzero integer polynomial is the positive greatest common divisor of its coefficients. The polynomial is primitive when its content is one. Gauss’s lemma states that the product of two primitive integer polynomials is primitive. Indeed, if a prime divided every coefficient of their product, reduction modulo that prime would give a product of two nonzero polynomials equal to zero in \(\mathbb F_p[x]\).

Clearing denominators and comparing contents gives the following consequence: a primitive polynomial in \(\mathbb Z[x]\) factors into positive degrees over \(\mathbb Q\) if and only if it does so over \(\mathbb Z\). If it is monic, the factors can be chosen monic. This is why coefficient divisibility, integer values, and bounds on roots can prove rational irreducibility.

The units of \(\mathbb Q[x]\) are the nonzero rational constants; the units of \(\mathbb Z[x]\) are \(\pm1\). Thus \(2x+2\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\), but is not an irreducible element of \(\mathbb Z[x]\). Removing the content avoids this distinction.

citations.note: Read with the author’s erratum to p. 10.

sections.title: The field generated by a root
sections.body:
If \(\alpha\) is algebraic over \(K\), its minimal polynomial \(m_\alpha\) is the unique monic irreducible polynomial in \(K[x]\) that vanishes at \(\alpha\). Every polynomial in \(K[x]\) vanishing at \(\alpha\) is divisible by \(m_\alpha\). The evaluation map gives

\[K(\alpha)\cong K[x]/(m_\alpha),\qquad [K(\alpha):K]=\deg m_\alpha.\]

In particular, an irreducible polynomial of degree \(n\) defines an extension of degree \(n\). If \(\alpha^3=2\), every element of \(\mathbb Q(\alpha)\) has a unique expression \(a+b\alpha+c\alpha^2\), with rational coefficients. Products reduce by \(\alpha^3=2\); inverses can be found by the Euclidean algorithm.

Adjoining a root does not usually give every root. The splitting field is the field generated by all roots. It is unique up to an isomorphism fixing \(K\), but can have much larger degree than the field generated by one root.

sections.title: Separable polynomials
sections.body:
A polynomial is separable if its roots in an algebraic closure are distinct. For a nonzero polynomial, this is equivalent to \(\gcd(f,f')=1\). An irreducible polynomial in characteristic zero is separable: its derivative is nonzero and has smaller degree, so it cannot share an irreducible factor with \(f\).

Positive characteristic requires more care. Over \(K=\mathbb F_p(t)\), the polynomial \(x^p-t\) is irreducible but has only one distinct root in an algebraic closure:

\[x^p-t=(x-t^{1/p})^p.\]

The extension \(K(t^{1/p})/K\) has degree \(p\), yet its only \(K\)-automorphism is the identity. By contrast, every irreducible polynomial over a finite field is separable. Fields for which every irreducible polynomial is separable are called perfect; characteristic-zero fields and finite fields are perfect.

citations.note: Separability, the derivative test, and perfect fields in the 2022 book.

sections.title: Factors and Galois orbits
sections.body:
Let \(f\in K[x]\) be separable, let \(L\) be its splitting field, and set \(G=\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)\). An element of \(G\) is a field automorphism of \(L\) fixing every element of \(K\). It permutes the roots, since \(f(\sigma\alpha)=\sigma(f(\alpha))=0\). This action is faithful because the roots generate \(L\).

Theorem

The root sets of the irreducible factors of \(f\) are exactly the orbits of \(G\). In particular, \(f\) is irreducible if and only if \(G\) acts transitively on its roots.

Proof

An automorphism fixing \(K\) sends a root to a root of its minimal polynomial. Conversely, two roots of the same irreducible factor define isomorphic extensions of \(K\), and that isomorphism extends to an automorphism of the splitting field. Thus the roots of each irreducible factor form one orbit.

If \(f\) has degree \(n\), numbering its roots identifies \(G\) with a subgroup of \(S_n\). A different numbering conjugates this subgroup. The permutation action records more than the abstract isomorphism type of the group: it records which roots and subsets of roots are related by automorphisms.

citations.note: The permutation action and its relation to factorization.

sections.title: Example
sections.body:
Example · \(x^3-2\)

Let \(\alpha=\sqrt[3]2\in\mathbb R\) and let \(\zeta\) be a primitive cube root of unity. The polynomial is Eisenstein at \(2\), and its roots are \(\alpha,\zeta\alpha,\zeta^2\alpha\). Its splitting field is \(L=\mathbb Q(\alpha,\zeta)\). Since \(\mathbb Q(\alpha)\) is real and \(\zeta\) is nonreal,

\[[L:\mathbb Q]=[L:\mathbb Q(\alpha)]\,[\mathbb Q(\alpha):\mathbb Q]=2\cdot3=6.\]

The Galois group is a subgroup of \(S_3\) of order six, hence is \(S_3\). Complex conjugation fixes \(\alpha\) and exchanges the two nonreal roots. An automorphism fixing \(\zeta\) sends \(\alpha\) to \(\zeta\alpha\) and cycles the three roots.

Over \(\mathbb Q(\zeta)\), the polynomial remains irreducible and has group \(C_3\). Over \(\mathbb Q(\alpha)\), it has a linear factor and an irreducible quadratic factor, and its splitting-field group is \(C_2\). These are subgroups of the original \(S_3\), obtained by requiring more elements to remain fixed.

citations.note: The cubic splitting field and its intermediate fields.

sections.title: Subfields and subgroups
sections.body:
The fundamental theorem of Galois theory makes this example systematic. For a finite Galois extension \(L/K\), intermediate fields \(K\subseteq E\subseteq L\) correspond to subgroups \(H\le G=\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)\):

\[E\longleftrightarrow\operatorname{Gal}(L/E),\qquad H\longleftrightarrow L^H.\]

Here \(L^H\) consists of the elements fixed by every member of \(H\). The correspondence reverses inclusion, and \([E:K]=[G:H]\). Moreover, \(E/K\) is Galois exactly when \(H\) is normal in \(G\); then \(\operatorname{Gal}(E/K)\cong G/H\).

For a root \(\alpha\) of an irreducible polynomial, the subgroup fixing \(\alpha\) corresponds to \(K(\alpha)\). Intermediate fields inside \(K(\alpha)\) correspond to subgroups containing this stabilizer. They also correspond to systems of blocks in the transitive action on the roots. This connects field arithmetic with primitivity, one of the main tools for proving that a Galois group is large.

citations.note: Blocks in transitive permutation groups and point stabilizers.

sections.title: Background
sections.body:
The classical problem was to solve equations by radicals. Galois theory replaces the search for a formula by a condition on a group: over a field of characteristic zero, a polynomial is solvable by radicals if and only if its Galois group is solvable. Thus an equation with group \(S_n\), for \(n\ge5\), has no expression for all its roots using only field operations and radicals. Particular equations of high degree can still be solvable; cyclotomic equations are a basic example.

Irreducibility criteria developed alongside this theory. Gauss’s lemma reduces rational factorization to integer factorization. Schönemann’s 1846 criterion and Eisenstein’s 1850 paper use divisibility by a prime. Dumas’s 1906 work organizes valuations through Newton polygons and combines information from several primes. These methods remain useful because they often give short proofs for entire families.

Reduction modulo primes provides a second connection with arithmetic. At a prime where the reduction is squarefree and its degree is unchanged, factor degrees give the cycle lengths of a Frobenius element. Chebotarev’s theorem describes how often conjugacy classes occur. This turns the factorization of a polynomial over finite fields into information about its Galois group over \(\mathbb Q\).

sections.title: Arithmetic and geometric connections
sections.body:
Over \(\mathbb F_q\), an irreducible polynomial of degree \(n\) defines \(\mathbb F_{q^n}\). This field already contains every root, and its Galois group is cyclic, generated by \(z\mapsto z^q\). Over \(\mathbb Q\), the corresponding root field need not be normal, and the group can be much larger. Finite-field factorization nevertheless supplies useful local information about rational polynomials.

Passing from \(\mathbb Q\) to \(\mathbb Q_p\) retains information lost by reduction modulo \(p\). Coefficient valuations determine Newton polygons; their slopes restrict degrees of local factors and ramification indices. A rational factor must satisfy these restrictions at every prime. Combining primes can therefore prove irreducibility even when no one prime does.

For a polynomial \(F(t,x)\), one can first study factorization and the Galois group over the function field \(K(t)\), then ask what happens after \(t\) is replaced by an element of \(K\). Hilbert irreducibility explains why many rational specializations preserve irreducibility. Over the complex numbers, analytic continuation of roots away from branch values gives a monodromy group; for a separable polynomial over \(\mathbb C(t)\), it agrees with the Galois group in its action on the roots.

In several variables, absolute irreducibility is also a geometric condition. Over an algebraically closed field, an irreducible polynomial generates a prime ideal and defines an irreducible reduced hypersurface. Newton polytopes, specialization, and factorization over function fields provide methods beyond the one-variable criteria.

citations.note: Hilbert irreducibility and Galois realizations.
Polynomial rings, prime ideals, and field extensions.

sections.title: Individual polynomials and families
sections.body:
For a specified polynomial over \(\mathbb Q\), exact algorithms can compute its irreducible factors and Galois group. A proof for a family is a different problem: it must cover all parameters in a stated range. Computations suggest a pattern and settle individual cases, but do not by themselves establish a uniform assertion.

The distinction is already visible in the group action. Irreducibility proves transitivity. To prove \(G\supseteq A_n\), one needs additional information, often primitivity and suitable cycles. Once this containment is known, the discriminant decides whether \(G=A_n\) or \(G=S_n\). A nonsquare discriminant alone gives only \(G\not\subseteq A_n\).

The remaining articles develop these steps for special families, compositions, random polynomials, and inverse Galois problems. The central reference for reducibility is Schinzel’s monograph; Prasolov gives a shorter treatment of many techniques, while Cox and Milne develop the field theory and group calculations.

questions.title: Does irreducibility imply a symmetric Galois group?
questions.body: No. The polynomial \(x^4+1=\Phi_8(x)\) is irreducible, but its splitting field is \(\mathbb Q(\zeta_8)\) and its group is \((\mathbb Z/8\mathbb Z)^\times\cong C_2\times C_2\), acting transitively on four roots. Its transitive group is a proper subgroup of the symmetric group.

citations.note: Cyclotomic extensions and their automorphism groups.

title: Reduction modulo primes
subject: criteria
summary: Factoring modulo primes gives restrictions on the degrees of rational factors. Incompatible restrictions prove irreducibility.
questionsAnswered: When does irreducibility modulo a prime imply irreducibility over Q?
How can factorizations modulo several primes prove irreducibility?
Can an irreducible rational polynomial be reducible modulo every prime?

sections.title: The reduction criterion
sections.body:
Theorem · reduction criterion

Let \(f\in\mathbb Z[x]\) be primitive of degree \(n\ge2\). If a prime \(p\) does not divide its leading coefficient and \(\bar f\in\mathbb F_p[x]\) is irreducible, then \(f\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\).

The leading-coefficient condition is essential. For example, \(2x^2+3x+1=(2x+1)(x+1)\) becomes the irreducible linear polynomial \(x+1\) modulo \(2\). Here reduction lowers the degree, so the criterion does not apply.

Proof

Gauss's lemma turns a rational factorization into \(f=gh\) in \(\mathbb Z[x]\). Since the product of the leading coefficients is not divisible by \(p\), both factors retain their positive degrees after reduction. Their reductions would factor \(\bar f\), a contradiction.

citations.note: Reduction modulo a prime and the Gauss-lemma proof.

sections.title: Factor-degree restrictions
sections.body:
Let \(f\in\mathbb Z[x]\) be primitive of degree \(n\), and let \(p\) not divide its leading coefficient. Factor its reduction into monic irreducible polynomials, recording each factor with its multiplicity. If their degrees are \(d_1,\ldots,d_r\), define

\[D_p=\left\{\sum_{i\in I}d_i:I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,r\}\right\}\cap\{1,\ldots,n-1\}.\]

Every proper rational factor of \(f\) has degree in \(D_p\). Indeed, Gauss’s lemma gives integral factors, their degrees are preserved modulo \(p\), and each reduced factor is a product of some of the listed irreducible factors.

If primes \(p_1,\ldots,p_s\) satisfy

\[D_{p_1}\cap\cdots\cap D_{p_s}=\varnothing,\]

then \(f\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\). It is enough to test degrees at most \(\lfloor n/2\rfloor\), since a reducible polynomial has a factor in that range. Repeated factors in a reduction are allowed in this degree argument; they must be counted with multiplicity.

citations.note: Reduction and coefficient methods for rational irreducibility; the subset-sum formulation follows directly from reduction of an integral factorization.

sections.title: Example
sections.body:
Example · \(f=x^4+x^3+x+2\)

\[\begin{aligned}f\bmod2&=x(x^3+x^2+1),\\ f\bmod3&=(x^2+1)(x^2+x-1).\end{aligned}\]

The cubic has no root in \(\mathbb F_2\), so it is irreducible there. The two quadratics have no roots in \(\mathbb F_3\), so they are irreducible there. Modulo \(2\), a proper rational factor could have degree \(1\) or \(3\). Modulo \(3\), it could only have degree \(2\). The sets are disjoint; hence \(f\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\).

citations.note: The reduction principle underlying the certificate; these two displayed factorizations are calculated for this entry.

sections.title: A polynomial reducible modulo every prime
sections.body:
The polynomial \(x^4+1\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\): translating by \(1\) gives \(x^4+4x^3+6x^2+4x+2\), Eisenstein at \(2\). Nevertheless it is reducible modulo every prime. At \(2\) it is \((x+1)^4\). For odd \(p\), its roots are primitive eighth roots of unity; since \(p^2\equiv1\pmod8\), they lie in \(\mathbb F_{p^2}\), so all irreducible factors have degree at most two.

In fact degree \(2\) remains compatible with every reduction, so even intersecting all the sets \(D_p\) does not prove irreducibility here. Indeed, \(C_2\times C_2\), the Galois group, contains no \(4\)-cycle. For a separable irreducible polynomial over \(\mathbb Q\), Chebotarev and the Frobenius factorization theorem show that an irreducible good reduction exists exactly when the group contains an \(n\)-cycle.

citations.note: A complementary quartic example and a proof that reduction at every prime can fail.
The relation between Frobenius conjugacy classes, factorization types, and Chebotarev density.

sections.title: Using other local information
sections.body: If a degree remains in every set \(D_p\) considered, these reductions have not excluded a factor of that degree. Newton polygons can give additional restrictions from coefficient valuations, including at primes where the reduction has repeated factors. Intersecting all the available degree sets may then prove irreducibility.

questions.title: Does every irreducible rational polynomial have an irreducible reduction?
questions.body: No. The precise condition is that the Galois group contain a full-length cycle. The polynomial \(x^4+1\) is a counterexample.

title: Schönemann–Eisenstein and Dumas criteria
subject: criteria
summary: Divisibility and coefficient valuations prove irreducibility by the Schönemann–Eisenstein and Dumas criteria. Translation provides further applications.
questionsAnswered: What are the hypotheses of the Schönemann–Eisenstein criterion?
When does a translation make the criterion apply?
How does the one-edge Dumas criterion extend Eisenstein’s criterion?

sections.title: The Schönemann–Eisenstein criterion
sections.body:
Theorem · Schönemann–Eisenstein

Let \(f=a_nx^n+\cdots+a_0\in\mathbb Z[x]\), with \(n\ge1\). Suppose a prime \(p\) satisfies \(p\nmid a_n\), \(p\mid a_i\) for \(0\le i\lt n\), and \(p^2\nmid a_0\). Then \(f\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\).

Proof

A factorization into positive degrees can be taken in \(\mathbb Z[x]\). Reducing it modulo \(p\) gives a factorization of the monomial \(a_nx^n\). Both reduced factors are monomials of positive degree, because their leading coefficients remain nonzero. Thus both original constant terms are divisible by \(p\), which would make \(a_0\) divisible by \(p^2\).

Schönemann's work of 1846 precedes Eisenstein's 1850 paper. Cox's historical account explains their different motivations and the connection with finite fields and the division of the lemniscate.

citations.note: Original historical source.
Eisenstein’s original treatment.
Historical attribution and the elementary form of the criterion.

sections.title: Changes of variable
sections.body:
For \(a\in K^\times\) and \(b\in K\), substitution \(x\mapsto ax+b\) is an automorphism of \(K[x]\) and preserves irreducibility. It may change the coefficient divisibility required by the criterion. Reversing coefficients, \(f^*(x)=x^{\deg f}f(1/x)\), also preserves irreducibility when \(f(0)\ne0\).

Example

\[(x+1)^4+1=x^4+4x^3+6x^2+4x+2.\]

The right side is Eisenstein at \(2\), proving irreducibility of \(x^4+1\). More generally, if \(p\) is prime,

\[\Phi_p(x+1)=\frac{(x+1)^p-1}{x}=\sum_{j=1}^{p}\binom pj x^{j-1}\]

is Eisenstein at \(p\): all intermediate binomial coefficients are divisible by \(p\), while the constant coefficient is exactly \(p\).

citations.note: The prime cyclotomic example after translation.

sections.title: Schönemann’s residue-power criterion
sections.body:
The following form allows a higher-degree irreducible factor in the reduction. Let \(\phi\in\mathbb Z[x]\) be monic with irreducible reduction modulo \(p\), let \(e\ge2\), and let \(M\in\mathbb Z[x]\) satisfy \(\deg M\lt e\deg\phi\) and \(\gcd(\bar\phi,\bar M)=1\). Then

\[f=\phi^e+pM\]

is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\). Indeed, a monic integral factorization would reduce to \(\bar g=\bar\phi^a\), \(\bar h=\bar\phi^b\), where \(a,b>0\) and \(a+b=e\). Write \(g=\phi^a+pg_1\), \(h=\phi^b+ph_1\). Comparing with \(f\), then dividing by \(p\) and reducing modulo \(p\), forces \(\bar\phi\mid\bar M\), a contradiction.

For example, \((x^2+x+1)^2+2=x^4+2x^3+3x^2+2x+3\) is irreducible: \(x^2+x+1\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb F_2\), and \(M=1\). The reduction is a power of an irreducible quadratic.

citations.note: Historical source of the residue-power criterion.
Modern statement of Schönemann’s criterion.

sections.title: The Dumas criterion
sections.body:
Theorem · one-edge Dumas criterion

Let \(f=a_nx^n+\cdots+a_0\in\mathbb Q_p[x]\), with \(a_0a_n\ne0\), \(v_p(a_n)=0\), and \(v_p(a_0)=k>0\). Suppose \(\gcd(n,k)=1\) and

\[v_p(a_i)\ge k\left(1-\frac{i}{n}\right)\qquad(0\lt i\lt n),\]

where \(v_p(0)=+\infty\). Then \(f\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q_p\). For a rational polynomial, this also proves irreducibility over \(\mathbb Q\).

The Newton polygon has one segment of slope \(-k/n\), so every root has valuation \(k/n\). A monic factor of degree \(d\) over \(\mathbb Q_p\) would have constant coefficient of valuation \(dk/n\), an integer. Coprimality forces \(n\mid d\). Hence no proper positive factor degree is possible. Eisenstein is the case \(k=1\).

citations.note: Classical source for the Newton-polygon criterion.
Introduction states Dumas’s criterion in reversed-coefficient form; the form here follows by coefficient reversal.
Roots and slopes over a discretely valued field.

sections.title: Example
sections.body:
Example · \(f=x^5+4x+4\)

At \(2\), the nonzero coefficient points are \((0,2),(1,2),(5,0)\). The middle point lies above the segment joining \((0,2)\) to \((5,0)\). Its slope is \(-2/5\), and \(\gcd(2,5)=1\). Thus \(f\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q_2\), hence over \(\mathbb Q\).

Eisenstein’s criterion at \(2\) does not apply because \(4\mid f(0)\). Dumas’s criterion instead uses the root valuation \(2/5\), whose denominator excludes every proper factor degree.

citations.note: The one-edge criterion used here; the valuation diagram and polynomial are an explicit worked computation.

sections.title: Limitations and translation
sections.body:
A Newton polygon with several slopes proves reducibility over \(\mathbb Q_p\), but not necessarily over \(\mathbb Q\). A single edge whose horizontal and vertical increments have a common divisor may correspond to either an irreducible or a reducible polynomial over \(\mathbb Q_p\). Other primes, residual polynomials, or a change of variable can give further information. Local irreducibility alone does not determine the global Galois group.

Even allowing every integral translation does not make the elementary Eisenstein test complete. Conrad proves that \(x^4-10x^2+1\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\), but \((x+c)^4-10(x+c)^2+1\) is never Eisenstein for any \(c\in\mathbb Z\). Thus translated Eisenstein criteria do not characterize irreducibility.

The stronger one-edge criterion succeeds after translation: at \(c=1\) the polynomial becomes \(x^4+4x^3-4x^2-16x-8\). Its \(2\)-adic coefficient valuations are \(3,4,2,2,0\), and the lower polygon is a single edge of slope \(-3/4\). Dumas therefore proves irreducibility even over \(\mathbb Q_2\).

citations.note: Irreducibility and failure of every integral Eisenstein shift.
The one-edge criterion applies to the translated quartic, whose coefficients and valuations are calculated here.
Distinct Newton slopes give factors over the complete local field; they do not imply reducibility over the rational field.

questions.title: Can an integral translation always make an irreducible polynomial Eisenstein?
questions.body: No. The irreducible polynomial \(x^4-10x^2+1\) is a counterexample. The counterexample concerns integral translations, and does not exclude other changes of variable or valuation criteria.

citations.note: Explicit counterexample. Proof in expository notes; this status records the unpublished source.

title: Newton polygons and Galois groups
subject: criteria
summary: Coefficient valuations determine root valuations and restrict factor degrees. Suitable Newton slopes also imply containment of the alternating group.
questionsAnswered: How do Newton slopes determine root valuations?
How can Newton polygons at several primes prove irreducibility?
How do residual polynomials give stronger factor-degree restrictions?
Which slope denominators force containment of A_n?

sections.title: Newton polygons and root valuations
sections.body:
Write \(f(x)=\sum_{i=0}^n a_ix^i\in\mathbb Q_p[x]\) with \(a_0a_n\ne0\), and normalize \(v_p(p)=1\). The Newton polygon is the lower convex hull of the points \((i,v_p(a_i))\) with \(a_i\ne0\). Zero coefficients have infinite valuation and contribute no finite points.

Theorem · slopes and roots

A segment of slope \(-u/v\), in lowest terms with \(v>0\), and horizontal length \(\ell\), corresponds to exactly \(\ell\) roots of valuation \(u/v\), counted with multiplicity. There is a factor over \(\mathbb Q_p\) consisting of all roots with each given valuation.

For a factor over \(\mathbb Q_p\), the number of its roots belonging to that slope must be a multiple of \(v\). Indeed, the constant coefficient of its corresponding monic slope factor has integer valuation. Thus the possible factor degrees are sums of multiples of the slope denominators, bounded by the lengths available on the respective segments.

citations.note: Definition and root–slope theorem.

sections.title: Combining primes
sections.body:
Let the Newton polygon at \(p\) have slopes \(-h_j/e_j\) in lowest terms, with \(e_j>0\), and horizontal lengths \(\ell_j\). Since the vertices have integer coordinates, \(e_j\) divides \(\ell_j\). A factor can use \(0,e_j,2e_j,\ldots,\ell_j\) roots from the \(j\)-th segment. Thus every proper factor over \(\mathbb Q_p\) has degree in

\[N_p=\left\{\sum_j e_j k_j: k_j\in\mathbb Z,\ 0\le k_j\le\ell_j/e_j\right\}\cap\{1,\ldots,n-1\}.\]

A rational factor is also a factor over every \(\mathbb Q_p\). Consequently, if \(N_{p_1}\cap\cdots\cap N_{p_s}\) is empty, then \(f\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\). These sets can also be intersected with degree restrictions obtained from factorizations modulo other primes.

The reason for the multiples of \(e_j\) is elementary once the root–slope theorem is known. A monic local factor made from \(d_j\) roots of valuation \(h_j/e_j\) has constant coefficient of valuation \(d_jh_j/e_j\). This is an integer, so \(e_j\mid d_j\). The degree-six example below gives \(N_2=\{2,4\}\) and \(N_3=\{3\}\), whose intersection is empty.

Dumas used several primes in this way; Bonciocat gives a systematic formulation and explicit criteria.

citations.note: Historical source for the polygon-product and several-prime method.
Systematic several-prime irreducibility criteria.

sections.title: Residual polynomials
sections.body:
The coefficients on a Newton edge also define a residual polynomial. It can exclude factor degrees permitted by the slope denominator.

Theorem · residual-polynomial criterion

Let \(f(x)=\sum_{i=0}^{ed}a_ix^i\in\mathbb Z_p[x]\) be monic. Suppose its Newton polygon is the single segment from \((0,hd)\) to \((ed,0)\), where \(h,e,d\) are positive integers and \(\gcd(h,e)=1\). Define

\[R_f(Y)=\sum_{j=0}^{d}\overline{\frac{a_{ej}}{p^{h(d-j)}}}\,Y^j\in\mathbb F_p[Y].\]

The polygon hypothesis makes every displayed quotient integral. If \(R_f\) is irreducible, then \(f\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q_p\).

Proof

In a monic factorization \(f=g_1g_2\) over \(\mathbb Q_p\), the factors have integral coefficients. All roots have valuation \(h/e\), so the constant coefficients show that the factor degrees are \(ed_1,ed_2\), with \(d_1+d_2=d\). The residual-polynomial product rule gives \(R_f=R_{g_1}R_{g_2}\), with degrees \(d_1,d_2\). This rule follows directly from coefficient multiplication: terms on the edge survive after normalization and reduction; terms above it vanish. If two indices summing to a multiple of \(e\) are individually not multiples of \(e\), their integral valuations put their product strictly above the edge. Irreducibility of \(R_f\) therefore forces one factor degree to be zero.

Example

For \(f=x^4+2x^2+4\) at \(p=2\), the points \((0,2),(2,1),(4,0)\) lie on one edge of slope \(-1/2\). Its denominator leaves a possible quadratic factor. Here \(h=1,e=2,d=2\), and

\[R_f(Y)=1+Y+Y^2.\]

This quadratic has no root in \(\mathbb F_2\). Thus \(f\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q_2\), and hence over \(\mathbb Q\), although its ordinary reduction is \(x^4\). The criterion does not assume tame ramification. When \(d=1\), it recovers the one-edge Dumas criterion.

citations.note: The product rule and residual-polynomial irreducibility criterion. The elementary specialization and quartic calculation are worked out here.
The same criterion is encoded by a complete type; the source explains its ramification and residue-degree information.

sections.title: Example
sections.body:
Example

\[F(x)=6!\sum_{j=0}^6\frac{x^j}{j!}=720+720x+360x^2+120x^3+30x^4+6x^5+x^6.\]

The coefficient valuations, from constant to leading term, are

\[\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrr}i&0&1&2&3&4&5&6\\\hline v_2(a_i)&4&4&3&3&1&1&0\\ v_3(a_i)&2&2&2&1&1&1&0\end{array}.\]

At \(2\), the vertices are \((0,4),(4,1),(6,0)\). The slopes are \(-3/4,-1/2\), with lengths \(4,2\). The only proper factor degrees permitted are \(2,4\). At \(3\), there is one segment from \((0,2)\) to \((6,0)\), with slope \(-1/3\); the only proper factor degree permitted is \(3\). Hence \(F\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\).

Coleman’s general treatment of exponential Taylor polynomials uses the same Newton-polygon method.

citations.note: Newton-polygon treatment of exponential Taylor polynomials; the degree-six valuation table is calculated here.
The local theorem justifying the factor-degree restrictions.

sections.title: A criterion for containing the alternating group
sections.body:
Theorem · a form of Hajir’s Newton-index criterion

Let \(f\in\mathbb Q[x]\) be irreducible of degree \(n\). Suppose a prime \(q\) divides the denominator, in lowest terms, of some Newton slope of \(f\) at a finite prime. If

\[\frac n2\lt q\le n-3,\]

then \(\operatorname{Gal}(f/\mathbb Q)\) contains \(A_n\).

The root valuation forces \(q\) to divide a ramification index in the local splitting field, and hence the order of the global group. Cauchy's theorem gives an element of order \(q\); because \(2q>n\), this element is a single \(q\)-cycle. Transitivity comes from irreducibility. A nontrivial block system would have both its block size and its number of blocks smaller than \(q\); an element of order \(q\) could act nontrivially on neither, which is impossible. Thus the action is primitive. Jordan's theorem then gives \(A_n\).

The discriminant decides between \(A_n\) and \(S_n\) only after this containment has been proved. A nonsquare discriminant alone does not imply the full symmetric group.

citations.note: Newton index divides the Galois-group order and a prime in the stated interval forces alternating-group containment.
Classical primitive-group theorem used in the final step.
Permutation-group background for primitivity and long prime cycles.

sections.title: Example
sections.body:
Example · \(f=x^8+2x^5+6\) has group \(S_8\)

Eisenstein at \(2\) proves irreducibility. At \(3\), the Newton polygon has vertices \((0,1),(5,0),(8,0)\), hence slopes \(-1/5,0\) of lengths \(5,3\). The denominator forces \(5\) to divide the Galois-group order. Since \(8\lt 2\cdot5\), an element of order \(5\) is a single 5-cycle. Irreducibility supplies transitivity, and \(8/2\lt 5\le8-3\) satisfies the criterion above. Thus the group contains \(A_8\).

The exact discriminant is

\[\operatorname{disc}(f)=2^{12}3^9\cdot79\cdot733.\]

It is nonsquare, so the group is \(S_8\). Here the reductions at \(2,3\) are \(x^8\) and \(x^5(x-1)^3\). Reading these multiplicities as Frobenius cycle lengths would be invalid.

citations.note: The Newton-index theorem proves alternating containment for the displayed octic. The valuations and resultant were computed exactly for this entry.
The discriminant-square criterion completes the group determination.

sections.title: Slope denominators and cycle lengths
sections.body:
A slope denominator need not be the length of a cycle in the Galois group. The prime-order argument above uses both the denominator and the interval \(n/2\lt q\le n-3\). If the relevant prime is smaller, an element of order \(q\) may be a product of several disjoint \(q\)-cycles. If irreducibility is unavailable, transitivity cannot be assumed.

Counterexample

The polynomial \(x^4+4=(x^2-2x+2)(x^2+2x+2)\) has one Newton slope \(-1/2\) at \(2\). Its roots are \(1\pm i,-1\pm i\), and its splitting field is \(\mathbb Q(i)\). The only nonidentity automorphism acts as a product of two transpositions, never a single transposition. Its discriminant \(2^{14}\) is a square, consistently with this even action. Capelli's exceptional fourth-power case explains the factorization.

The same phenomenon occurs for irreducible polynomials. The irreducible quartic \(x^4+2x^2+4\) certified above also has slope denominator two. Its roots are \((\pm\sqrt2\pm\sqrt{-6})/2\), with independent sign choices, and its splitting field is \(\mathbb Q(\sqrt2,\sqrt{-6})\). Its Galois group is \(V_4\) in the transitive degree-four action: all three nonidentity elements are double transpositions. Its discriminant \(2^{10}3^2\) is a square.

For Laguerre and Taylor polynomials, explicit coefficient formulas make the Newton polygons accessible. The resulting factor-degree restrictions prove irreducibility in many cases, and suitable slopes then give alternating-group containment.

citations.note: The irreducibility input and prime interval are explicit hypotheses.
The fourth-power exception explains the explicitly factored quartic.
The earlier residual-polynomial criterion proves irreducibility of the second counterexample; its radicals, field, permutation action, and discriminant are calculated here.

related.why: Eisenstein corresponds to one edge of slope −1/n.

Cauchy’s and Jordan’s theorems turn suitable ramification divisors into alternating containment.
After alternating containment, the discriminant determines whether the group is alternating or symmetric.
The binomials x⁶−72 and x⁴+4 exhibit power obstructions and valuation constraints.
Factorial and binomial coefficient formulas determine useful Newton slopes.

questions.title: How can one refine Newton-polygon restrictions on factor degrees?
questions.scope: Local factorization of a specified separable polynomial over a p-adic field
questions.body: Residual polynomials give the first refinement, illustrated above. If a residual factor is repeated, that stage may leave irreducibility undecided; higher Newton polygons refine the associated valuation and residue data. The Guàrdia–Montes–Nart theory gives a terminating local factorization procedure for separable polynomials. Finding shorter irreducibility proofs for particular families remains a separate question.

title: Root bounds and prime-value criteria
subject: criteria
summary: Perron’s criterion uses the size of coefficients to locate roots. Prime-value criteria combine integer evaluations with root bounds or digit conditions.
questionsAnswered: When does Perron’s coefficient inequality prove irreducibility?
Which root bound makes one prime value sufficient?
What does Cohn’s theorem say about the digits of a prime?

sections.title: Perron’s criterion
sections.body:
Theorem · Perron

Let \(f=x^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_0\in\mathbb Z[x]\), where \(n\ge2\) and \(a_0\ne0\). If

\[|a_{n-1}|>1+\sum_{i=0}^{n-2}|a_i|,\]

then \(f\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\).

Proof

On \(|z|=1\), the term \(a_{n-1}z^{n-1}\) strictly dominates the sum of all other terms. Rouché's theorem gives exactly \(n-1\) roots inside the unit circle and one outside. If the monic polynomial factored over \(\mathbb Z\), one positive-degree monic factor would have all roots strictly inside. Its constant coefficient would be a nonzero integer whose absolute value is the product of numbers smaller than one, an impossibility.

citations.note: Original source for coefficient-dominance irreducibility.
A modern presentation of Perron’s criterion.

sections.title: Example
sections.body:
Example · \(x^5+3x+1\)

Its reciprocal polynomial is

\[f^*(x)=x^5f(1/x)=x^5+3x^4+1.\]

Now \(3>1+1\), so Perron's criterion proves \(f^*\) irreducible. Since the constant term of \(f\) is nonzero, coefficient reversal preserves factorizations and proves \(f\) irreducible. The same argument works for \(x^n+3x+1\) for every \(n\ge2\).

citations.note: Coefficient-dominance theorem; the reversal and worked family are direct applications.

sections.title: A prime-value criterion
sections.body:
Theorem · prime-value criterion

Let \(f\in\mathbb Z[x]\) be nonconstant. Suppose an integer \(m\) satisfies \(|f(m)|\) prime and \(|m-\alpha|>1\) for every complex root \(\alpha\) of \(f\). Then \(f\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\).

In an integral factorization \(f=gh\), each positive-degree factor has an integer leading coefficient \(b\ne0\), so

\[|g(m)|=|b|\prod_{g(\alpha)=0}|m-\alpha|>1.\]

Both factors would therefore give integer divisors of \(f(m)\) larger than one in absolute value. A practical sufficient condition is a certified root bound \(|\alpha|\le R\) and \(|m|>R+1\).

For example, the roots of \(x^4-10x^2+1\) are \(\pm\sqrt2\pm\sqrt3\), all of absolute value less than \(4\). At \(m=6\), the value is \(937\), a prime. Every distance is greater than \(2\), so the criterion proves irreducibility. Primality can be checked by the primes at most \(\sqrt{937}\lt 31\).

citations.note: Prime evaluations together with root or coefficient bounds; the displayed distance criterion is proved in the text.
The roots of the quartic used in the example.

sections.title: Cohn’s criterion
sections.body:
Cohn's decimal theorem says that if \(p=a_n10^n+\cdots+a_0\) is prime, with \(n\ge1\), \(0\le a_i\le9\), and \(a_n\ne0\), then \(a_nx^n+\cdots+a_0\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\). Brillhart, Filaseta, and Odlyzko extend the result to arbitrary integer bases \(b\ge2\), again assuming a nonconstant digit polynomial. The digit restrictions are essential to this statement; a prime value alone does not imply irreducibility.

For instance, \(101\) is prime, so its decimal digits give the irreducible polynomial \(x^2+1\). The unrestricted prime-value inference fails for \((x-1)(x+1)\), which takes the prime value \(3\) at \(x=2\), and is reducible.

citations.note: Cohn’s theorem, prime-value root separation, and extension beyond decimal digits.
A further exposition and proof of the arbitrary-base extension.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.body:
The two arguments use integrality in different ways. Perron’s criterion would force a factor to have a nonzero constant coefficient of absolute value less than one. In the prime-value criterion, each nonconstant factor would take an integer value of absolute value greater than one at the chosen point. Both conclusions contradict a factorization in \(\mathbb Z[x]\).

Neither argument follows from real-rootedness alone. For example, \(x^2-1\) has only real roots and is reducible.

citations.note: General reducibility theory and criteria for special forms.
Exact polynomial factorization algorithms.

sections.title: A prime constant term
sections.body:
Let \(f=a_0+\sum_{i=1}^r a_i x^{n_i}\in\mathbb Z[x]\) be primitive, with nonzero coefficients and \(0\[C=\gcd_i\bigl(x^{n_i}+\operatorname{sgn}(a_0a_i)\bigr),\]

with monic gcd. Then \(C\) is the cyclotomic part, and \(f/C\) is irreducible and nonreciprocal. Thus \(f\) is irreducible exactly when \(C=1\).

Every root has modulus at least \(1\). The prime constant term forces all but one irreducible factor to have constant term \(\pm1\); those factors are cyclotomic. Equality in the triangle inequality identifies their gcd.

For positive coefficients, irreducibility is equivalent to the \(n_i\) not all having the same \(2\)-adic valuation. For example, \(3+x+x^2+x^5\) is irreducible.

citations.note: Primitivity is included explicitly to remove constant-content degeneracies.

related.why: Root bounds can prove irreducibility when every prime reduction is reducible.
Coefficient reversal can put the dominant coefficient in the required position.
Sparse support simplifies root and coefficient-norm estimates.
A family criterion can give a short proof without general factorization.

questions.title: Does one prime value prove irreducibility?
questions.scope: Integer polynomials without additional coefficient or root restrictions
questions.body: No: \((x-1)(x+1)\) takes the prime value \(3\) at \(x=2\). A distance-to-roots bound, a sufficiently large evaluation, or digit restrictions can turn a prime value into an irreducibility criterion.

citations.note: Precise additional hypotheses for prime-value arguments.

title: Sparse polynomials and factor reversal
subject: criteria
summary: For polynomials with two widely separated blocks of coefficients, large-gap theorems prove irreducibility of the nonreciprocal part under explicit hypotheses.
questionsAnswered: Which reciprocal factors must be separated in a large-gap theorem?
What information is preserved when a factor is reversed?
Under what hypotheses is the nonreciprocal part eventually irreducible?

sections.title: Large gaps and reciprocal factors
sections.body:
Consider the family

\[f_N(x)=x^N c(x^{-1})+d(x),\qquad N>\deg c+\deg d,\]

where \(c,d\in\mathbb Z[x]\) are fixed and \(c(0)d(0)\ne0\). The high and low blocks of coefficients are separated by a gap. Write \(h^*(x)=x^{\deg h}h(1/x)\). A nonconstant irreducible factor is reciprocal when \(h^*=\pm h\); the nonreciprocal part is obtained by removing all such irreducible factors, including their multiplicities.

Cyclotomic polynomials are reciprocal up to sign, but other reciprocal factors can occur. Thus irreducibility of the nonreciprocal part proves irreducibility of the original polynomial only after all reciprocal factors have been excluded.

citations.note: Lacunary polynomial factorization and reciprocal factors.
Large-gap notation and definitions.

sections.title: Schinzel’s theorem
sections.body:
Call \((c,d)\) Capellian if \(-d(x)/c(x^{-1})\) is a \(p\)-th power in \(\mathbb Q(x)\) for some prime \(p\), or if \(d(x)/c(x^{-1})\) is four times a fourth power. These power conditions lead to factorizations for infinitely many exponents.

Theorem · Schinzel, in large-gap form

Assume \(c(0)d(0)\ne0\), \(\gcd_{\mathbb Z[x]}(c^*,d)=1\), \(c\ne\pm d\), and that \((c,d)\) is not Capellian. Then there is an effective bound \(N_0\), depending on \(c,d\), such that for \(N>N_0\) the nonreciprocal part of \(f_N\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\).

This is the formulation in Sawin–Shusterman–Stoll, Theorem 1.2, deduced there from Schinzel’s work. Filaseta–Ford–Konyagin improve explicit thresholds. Sawin–Shusterman–Stoll give further bounds and algorithms under an additional robustness hypothesis (Theorems 1.5–1.6).

citations.note: The general lacunary result behind this formulation.
Improved effective bounds with explicit exclusions.
Exact hypotheses of the large-gap theorem and the extra robustness assumption for its improved bound.

sections.title: Factor reversal
sections.body:
For \(f(0)\ne0\) and a factorization \(f=gh\), form \(G=gh^*\). The reciprocal product does not change:

\[GG^*=ff^*.\]

Equivalently, as Laurent polynomials, one may use \(g(x)h(x^{-1})\); multiplication by a power of \(x\) only changes the presentation. On the unit circle, a real-coefficient polynomial satisfies \(|h^*(z)|=|h(z)|\). Consequently \(G\) and \(f\) have the same squared coefficient norm, by Parseval's identity:

\[\sum_j |[x^j]G|^2=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|G(e^{it})|^2\,dt=\sum_j |[x^j]f|^2.\]

For a sparse polynomial with small integral coefficients, the right side is small. Only finitely many multisets of nonzero integer coefficients have that norm, although their positions may vary. Comparing the full identity \(GG^*=ff^*\) then restricts the possible positions as well as the coefficients. In suitable sparse families, these restrictions exclude nonreciprocal factorizations. Ljunggren’s method and its later extensions use this restriction.

citations.note: Original factor-reversal approach to sparse trinomials and quadrinomials.
Small Euclidean coefficient norm as a factorization constraint.
Reversal identity and the later algorithmic development.

sections.title: Example
sections.body:
Example · \(x^N+x+1\)

Let \(\zeta\) be a primitive cube root of unity. Since \(\zeta+1=-\zeta^2\),

\[\zeta^N+\zeta+1=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad N\equiv2\pmod3.\]

Thus \(x^2+x+1\) divides \(x^N+x+1\) exactly in that residue class. In degree \(5\), for example,

\[x^5+x+1=(x^2+x+1)(x^3-x^2+1).\]

The cubic has no rational root, hence is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\). Thus infinitely many members are reducible because of a recurring cyclotomic factor.

The periodicity is general for a fixed cyclotomic factor: evaluation at a root of unity depends on \(N\) modulo its order. The large-gap literature combines this elementary observation with bounds that control other factors.

citations.note: Sparse trinomial factorization and reciprocal obstructions; the displayed root-of-unity calculation is given here.
Effective eventual description by finitely many exceptional exponents and arithmetic progressions.

sections.title: A family with an exceptional degree
sections.body:
Sawin–Shusterman–Stoll prove that \(x^N-7x^2+1\) is irreducible for every \(N\ge5\), and also for \(N=3\). The degree \(4\) is exceptional:

\[x^4-7x^2+1=(x^2-3x+1)(x^2+3x+1).\]

Their general theory supplies an eventual threshold, and a finite check handles the remaining exponents in this example.

citations.note: The complete k=7 example and its exceptional quartic.

related.why: Large-gap theorems concern the nonreciprocal part.
Trinomials give examples of factor reversal and recurring cyclotomic factors.
Coefficient norms and root bounds supplement coefficient-dominance criteria.
Capellian obstructions are binomial power obstructions over a rational function field.

questions.title: How small can a uniform large-gap threshold be?
questions.scope: Pairs satisfying the hypotheses of the large-gap theorem; degree sum δ and squared coefficient weight at most w
questions.body: Sawin–Shusterman–Stoll define \(N_{\mathrm{opt}}(\delta,w)\) as the smallest uniform threshold for their Theorem 1.2 over pairs with \(\deg c+\deg d=\delta\) and \(\|c\|_2^2+\|d\|_2^2\le w\). Their Question 1.7 asks, for fixed \(\delta>1\), whether this is \(O_\delta(\log w)\); Question 1.8 asks for the uniform bound \(O(\delta\log w)\). This records the questions as posed in that paper; it is not a claim that all later work has been excluded.
